title: Three-needle cast-off
subtitle: Joining two live edges into a seam in one row.
excerpt: The three-needle cast-off (UK) or three-needle bind-off (US) knits matching stitches from two needles together and casts them off simultaneously, producing a neat, secure seam without sewing.
sourceNotes: Method described in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) as a joining cast-off. Weldon's Practical Knitter (1886) references a similar two-needle joining technique for shoulder seams.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique that joins two sets of live stitches into a seam by knitting one stitch from each needle together, then casting off as you go. UK name for the three-needle bind-off.

content.text: (abbreviated 3-ndl co; US: three-needle bind-off) closes two sets of live stitches into a single seam without a darning needle or sewing. The method works by knitting one stitch from the front needle and one from the back needle together, then casting off as you would a standard row. It produces a ridge on the outside of the join; turning the work so the wrong sides face outward before starting hides the ridge inside the finished piece. Difficulty: intermediate, because it requires three needles in play at once.
Two needle tips or short circular needles, each holding one set of live stitches
One extra straight needle or the cable of a circular needle as the working needle
Both sets of live stitches must be the same count
Hold the two needles parallel, with right sides facing each other (wrong sides out) if you want the ridge hidden on the inside.
Insert the working needle from left to right through the first stitch on the front needle and the first stitch on the back needle at once.
Wrap the yarn and draw a loop through both stitches. Slip both stitches off their needles. One stitch is on the working needle.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 for the next pair. Two stitches are on the working needle.
Pass the first stitch on the working needle over the second and off, as in the standard cast-off. One stitch remains.
Repeat steps 2-5 to the end. Fasten off the last stitch.

Shoulder seams on yoked and set-in-sleeve garments are the classic use. Toe grafting on socks traditionally uses Kitchener stitch, but the three-needle cast-off is used when a visible ridge at the toe is acceptable. It also joins pocket linings to body stitches, and closes the live stitches at the top of a hood.

items.symptom: Ridge appears on the right side of the finished piece
items.cause: Wrong sides were facing each other rather than right sides
items.fix: For a hidden ridge, place right sides together (wrong sides out) before starting. The ridge will sit on the inside of the seam.

items.cause: Knitting the paired stitches too tightly
items.fix: Use a needle one size larger for the cast-off, or consciously work loose stitches at step 3.

items.cause: Different number of stitches on each needle
items.fix: The three-needle cast-off requires exactly equal stitch counts. If counts differ, increase or decrease on the final body row before beginning the join.
